results.fact: total elevation loss vs. gain and vs. the itinerary's own days
results.evidence: The contradiction is real: loss_ft is 13000 against gain_ft 6200 on an out-and-back from one trailhead. No two sources give a cumulative gain for East Fury alone. One 4-day trip report gives ~42 mi and 13,000 ft gained and lost, but that trip also climbed Luna Peak. A 2024 survey trip gives 54 mi and 15,000 ft with a different walk-in. A third trip, which also traversed to West Fury, gives only an elevation range (1,640-8,280 ft). The row's own waypoints imply ~9,000+ ft of cumulative gain (lake 1,600 -> Luna Pass 7,200 with the col traverse, the drop to ~6,500 ft and the climb to 8,300+, the regain to Luna Pass, and the climb from the lake back up to the 2,150 ft trailhead). So gain_ft 6200 and the itinerary day gains (6,900) also look low, and loss_ft 13000 appears to be the total for the trip that included Luna. Also note that the last sentence of descent_text credits its 42-mile/13,000-ft figure to 'a published trip report', which is a source mention, and that trip included Luna Peak.

Round-trip figures from independent trips are 41 mi (East and West Fury, water taxi) and 42 mi (East Fury and Luna Peak), so ~42 is within rounding of totalNote's '~35-40 mi'. The itinerary's 35 mi counts walked trail miles only and leaves out the boat crossing. That is a different convention, not an incompatible fact. The descent_text sentence that carries the 42-mile figure is flagged under the gain/loss result, because it cites a trip report and describes a trip that included Luna.
dist_km 27.4 km = 17.0 mi, exactly the one-way approach the approach prose states. dist_km is the one-way approach figure on screen, so the two agree.

The contradiction is real: gain_ft is 4799 against itinerary days of 7,200 and a totalNote of 6,500-7,000. Sources do not agree on a cumulative figure. One NE Buttress trip report gives ~4,700 ft 'each direction', which is the net trailhead-to-summit difference and appears to be where 4,799 comes from. A ski trip via Bridge Creek gives 5,300 ft, and a trip combining Goode and Logan gives 20,000 ft. By the row's own geometry (trailhead ~4,500 ft, down the PCT to ~2,800 ft, camp ~6,700 ft, summit 9,220 ft, then ~1,700 ft back up the PCT) the cumulative gain is ~8,000+ ft, so all three stored figures may be low. The itinerary also leaves out the PCT loss on day 1 and the regain on day 3.

results.fact: whether the route crosses the Goode Glacier / has crevasse hazard
results.correct_value: The North Fork approach crosses glacier ice below the couloir, with crevasse, snow-bridge and bergschrund hazard.
results.evidence: A 2015 trip report of the Southwest Couloir via Bridge Creek describes downclimbing onto a small glacier below 8,000 ft on the way to the couloir, carrying crampons, axe and rope. A 2003 NE Buttress party descended the SW Couloir back to the North Fork side: they rappelled from the Storm King-Goode col onto the glacier, then passed a bergschrund and a steep, icy, broken section. A third report describes crossing a glacier remnant to reach the couloir. The row's waypoints, approach, obj_haz and approach_variants ('hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft') already agree. seasonal_hazards.crevasses and the avalanche zone's 'non-glaciated' label are the outliers.
